source.title: Dichotomy of Early and Late Phase Implicit Biases Can Provably Induce Grokking
source.authors: Kaifeng Lyu; Jikai Jin; Zhiyuan Li; S. S. Du; Jason D. Lee; Wei Hu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present and readable, with minor OCR/math formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports grokking on modular addition using a two-layer ReLU network and full-batch gradient descent, a different training setup from the original work. It also tests how initialization scale and weight decay affect the transition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on modular addition, sparse linear classification, misgrokking, matrix completion, and training without weight decay. Curves for initialization-scale and weight-decay comparisons are shown in figures; the text describes their overall trends but does not give exact transition values. Claims cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces modular-addition grokking with a two-layer ReLU net under full-batch GD, a different setup from the originals. It varies initialization scale and weight decay, and adds theory plus synthetic diagonal-net and matrix-completion examples. Its own results bear on V1, V3 and V5, and on the adaptive-optimizer part of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that large initialization plus small nonzero weight decay gives a long kernel-predictor phase, then a provably sharp transition near (1/λ)log α toward KKT points of min-norm/max-margin problems. Grokking results when the late predictor generalizes better, and misgrokking when it generalizes worse. They add that other late biases (margin maximization without weight decay, sharpness reduction) can also cause grokking with a less sharp transition.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the same modular-addition task but a two-layer ReLU network trained with full-batch gradient descent; also studies synthetic sparse classification and matrix completion, with theoretical gradient-flow analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that larger initialization delays the modular-addition transition, smaller weight decay delays it, and sufficiently strong weight decay can hinder training and eventually collapse training accuracy. Without weight decay, test accuracy improves much more slowly and the transition is not sharp.

fits_no_version.finding: On multiplication-table matrix completion (5% of entries observed), training loss is minimized in ~10^1 steps but the sharp test-loss transition comes after ~10^6 steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like delays in test loss occur in overparameterized matrix completion under large init and small weight decay.

record.problems: Experimental curves are presented without reported uncertainty estimates. The main theorem gives a KKT condition in the classification rich regime, which is not sufficient for global optimality in general; the authors explicitly note this limitation. The paper does not test dataset-size dependence of the delay.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size; only a 40% split is used.
Not tested: no circuit formation, memorization removal or mechanistic progress measures.
No realistic image, text or molecule data; the MNIST/IMDB results are cited from Liu et al., not run here.
Not tested: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Critical dataset size and ungrokking below it are not tested; there is no circuit-efficiency measurement.
Not tested: algorithms are not compared across runs.
Floating-point or softmax numerical artifacts are not examined.

missing.what: Comparison row for the weight-decay sweep: larger λ makes the transition earlier; above a threshold training accuracy collapses; smaller λ delays it.
Theoretical sample-complexity contrast: the max L2-margin classifier needs O(kd) samples while the max L1-margin classifier needs O(k² log d). This bears on a data-size dependence of the delay.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked r6 to no version, but misgrokking bears directly on V5's claim that the low-norm bias favours generalization, so I relinked it. The V7 verdict covers only the optimizer and instability part; softmax precision is untested. Figure-only rows give no transition times, so the V3 verdicts rest on the text's comparative statements. Linking r5 to V3 is generous, since the data are synthetic rather than the realistic domains V3 names.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not sweep training-set size to test whether the delay grows as the dataset shrinks.
It analyzes early and late implicit biases, but does not test the formation of an identifiable generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, or continuous mechanistic progress measures.

The paper tests initialization scale and weight decay on modular addition, and reports a synthetic sparse-linear example. It does not test realistic image, text, or molecule data, or directly sweep weight norm.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.

The paper studies transitions between kernel and min-norm/max-margin predictors and gives a sparse-classification example, but does not establish a critical dataset size or test an efficiency account based on identifiable circuits.
It does not compare algorithms learned across runs or test convergence to the same identifiable algorithm.
It does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU net
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent on modular addition with cross-entropy loss.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy over training steps
rows.value: Training accuracy reaches 100% in 10⁶ steps while test accuracy remains close to random guessing; after one additional order of magnitude in steps, test accuracy jumps to 100%.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the training and test accuracy trajectory; the plot gives the curves.
rows.check: For V7 the row shows the delay persisting under plain full-batch GD with no adaptive optimizer. The artifact-disappearance effect V7 predicts is absent here; 'observed' applies to V1 only.

source_check.correct: V1: observed. V7: absent for the predicted disappearance under nonadaptive optimization; delayed generalization persists under full-batch GD.

rows.subject: two-layer diagonal linear net
rows.operation_detail: Training on synthetic sparse linear classification with large initialization and weight decay.

conditions.value: n=256 samples uniformly from {±1}^d; 3-sparse ground truth

rows.value: The model fits the training set quickly but initially fails to generalize; after a sharp late transition, test accuracy becomes 100%.
rows.note: The authors explain the contrast as early max L2-margin versus late max L1-margin behavior; their generalization bounds give different sample-complexity rates for these predictors.
rows.check: The data are synthetic sparse ±1 vectors, not the images, text or molecules V3 names. It bears on V3 only as non-modular-arithmetic data; the setting should be noted on the row.

rows.subject: two-layer diagonal linear net
rows.operation_detail: Training on a synthetic Gaussian linear-classification task with a large L2-margin.

conditions.value: 32 samples from the described Gaussian-separated distribution

rows.value: The model first reaches 100% test accuracy; after longer training, test accuracy drops to nearly 50%.
rows.note: The authors call this reversal “misgrokking”; it is not evidence for the delayed rise to near-perfect test accuracy specified by the claim versions.
rows.check: Misgrokking: the late low-norm (max L1-margin) bias destroys generalization, test accuracy falling from 100% to ~50%. This bears directly on V5's claim that the low-norm bias favours the generalizing solution. It should not be ['none'].

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU net
rows.operation_detail: Modular-addition training without weight decay, using a learning rate adjusted to keep the trajectory close to gradient flow.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy over continuous time
rows.value: Test accuracy slowly transitions from ∼0% to 100% as t increases from 10¹⁰ to 10¹⁴; the transition is described as no longer sharp.
rows.note: The delayed improvement occurs, but without weight decay the transition is much less sharp and takes far longer than in the weight-decay experiment.
rows.check: With λ=0, the delayed rise still occurs but is gradual over 10^10 to 10^14 time units. For V3 this means removing weight decay lengthens the delay rather than switching it off. For V7, the learning rate is kept near gradient flow to exclude instability, yet the delay persists (absent for V7's predicted disappearance).

source_check.correct: Test accuracy gradually rises from approximately 0% to 100% over continuous times 10^(10^2) to 10^(10^4). V1: partial. V7: absent for the predicted disappearance when optimizer instability is controlled. This experiment does not establish V3's initialization/weight-norm on/off claim.

rows.subject: homogeneous neural nets (theoretical setting)
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of the predictor direction under large initialization and small nonzero weight decay.

conditions.value: αθ̄init with α large and zero initial output
classification and regression under stated assumptions

rows.baseline: early kernel predictor based on NTK features
rows.value: The analysis proves a sharp transition near λ⁻¹ log α toward a KKT solution of a neural-net min-norm/max-margin problem; the paper notes this need not be globally optimal in general.
rows.note: This supports the paper’s low-norm/max-margin implicit-bias account, but does not establish the critical dataset-size prediction or identify an efficient circuit.
rows.check: This is a theorem, not an empirical measurement. It proves a sharp kernel-to-KKT(min-norm) transition near (1/λ)log α, but only KKT points, not global optima. It should be flagged as theory rather than a measured result.
